pack.description: Build a Sentence — reorder chunks to complete a natural reply. Pattern mix follows the PRD internal curriculum weights (not an ETS distribution).
pack.copyright_policy: Original synthetic content. No operational ETS item copied.

exercises.context: Did Professor Miller say when the revised report is due?
exercises.full_response: She said that we should submit the revised report by Friday.
exercises.explanation: Reported speech uses statement order (subject + verb): "that we should submit", never the question order "should we submit".

exercises.context: Do you know when the library opens tomorrow?
exercises.full_response: No, but I'll ask the librarian when it opens.
exercises.explanation: Inside an embedded question there is no auxiliary "do": "when it opens", not "when does it open".

exercises.context: Why was Maria at the registrar's office?
exercises.full_response: She wanted to know whether her transcript had been sent.
exercises.explanation: "Wanted to know whether" + subject + verb. The inverted form "had her transcript been" belongs only in a direct question.

exercises.context: What did the interviewer ask you?
exercises.full_response: She asked what I found most challenging.
exercises.explanation: Reported wh-questions keep statement order and drop "did": "what I found".

exercises.context: Have you decided on a topic for your paper yet?
exercises.full_response: Not yet. I'm still wondering which of the two topics would be easier to research.
exercises.explanation: The wh-phrase "which of the two topics" is the subject of the embedded clause, followed directly by its verb "would be".

exercises.context: The seminar room was locked this morning.
exercises.full_response: Could you tell me who has the key to it?
exercises.explanation: When "who" is the subject, the verb follows it directly: "who has the key". The question mark belongs to "Could you tell me…".

exercises.context: Is the conference still happening next week?
exercises.full_response: I have no idea whether it has been postponed or not.
exercises.explanation: "Whether … or not" and "whether or not …" are both correct; the clause keeps statement order (it has been).

exercises.context: Why are you calling the bookstore?
exercises.full_response: I need to find out how much the new edition will cost.
exercises.explanation: After "find out", use wh-word + subject + auxiliary + verb: "how much the new edition will cost".

exercises.context: What did your advisor want to know?
exercises.full_response: He asked me where I was planning to apply after graduation.
exercises.explanation: Reported question: "where I was planning" (statement order), not "where was I planning".

exercises.context: Why is everyone so worried about the final exam?
exercises.full_response: There's a rumor that it will include material from the optional readings.
exercises.explanation: A noun-complement clause (rumor that + complete clause) states the content of the rumor; "which" would need a gap in the clause.

exercises.context: Why did they cancel the field trip?
exercises.full_response: The main reason was that the bus company could not provide a driver.
exercises.explanation: "The reason was that + clause" is the standard written form.

exercises.context: What surprised you most in the results?
exercises.full_response: The fact that so few participants noticed the change surprised me.
exercises.explanation: The whole phrase "The fact that … the change" is the subject; the main verb "surprised" comes after it.

exercises.context: Has the department made a decision about the new course?
exercises.full_response: Not yet, but there's a good chance that it will be approved.
exercises.explanation: "A good chance that + clause": the course will be approved (passive), so "it will" alone would leave the clause incomplete.

exercises.context: Which professor are you taking for statistics?
exercises.full_response: The one whose lectures are posted online.
exercises.explanation: "Whose" shows possession (the professor's lectures); "who's" means "who is".

exercises.context: Did you find the article you needed?
exercises.full_response: Yes, the librarian showed me a database that I hadn't heard of.
exercises.explanation: The relative clause follows its noun (a database that…) and keeps the stranded preposition at the end (heard of).

exercises.context: Who is giving the keynote speech at the conference?
exercises.full_response: A researcher whose work on climate migration has been widely cited.
exercises.explanation: The subject of the relative clause is "whose work on climate migration" (singular), so the verb is "has been".

exercises.context: Why did you choose this university?
exercises.full_response: It was the only one that offered the program I wanted.
exercises.explanation: After "the only one", use "that" as subject of the relative clause; "the program I wanted" is a reduced relative (object "that" omitted).

exercises.context: How did the meeting with your supervisor go?
exercises.full_response: She encouraged me to submit the paper to a journal.
exercises.explanation: "Encourage" takes object + to-infinitive: encourage someone to do something.

exercises.context: Are you still working at the café?
exercises.full_response: No, I stopped working there last month.
exercises.explanation: "Stop + -ing" means to end an activity; "stop + to-infinitive" means to pause in order to do something else.

exercises.context: Did you remember to email the professor about the project?
exercises.full_response: Yes, and she suggested that we meet on Thursday.
exercises.explanation: "Suggest" is followed by a that-clause with the base verb (subjunctive: we meet), never "suggest us to meet".

exercises.context: Why isn't Sam at the seminar?
exercises.full_response: He must have forgotten about the schedule change.
exercises.explanation: Deduction about the past: modal + have + past participle (must have forgotten).

exercises.context: Was it a good idea to take five courses this semester?
exercises.full_response: Probably not. I should have taken fewer.
exercises.explanation: Past regret: should have + past participle. "Courses" are countable, so "fewer", not "less".

exercises.context: How long have you been studying Japanese?
exercises.full_response: I have been studying it since my second year.
exercises.explanation: Present perfect continuous with "since" + starting point; "for" requires a duration.

exercises.context: Are you going to the conference in Chicago?
exercises.full_response: I would go if my department covered the registration fee.
exercises.explanation: Second conditional: would + base verb in the main clause, past simple in the if-clause.

exercises.context: Did you hear that the trip was cancelled?
frame: , I wouldn't have bought the tickets.
exercises.full_response: Had I known about it earlier, I wouldn't have bought the tickets.
exercises.explanation: Inverted third conditional: "Had I known" = "If I had known". "If I known" is ungrammatical.

exercises.context: What happens if I miss the lab session?
exercises.full_response: Unless you have a medical note from the clinic, you will lose the points.
exercises.explanation: "Unless" already means "if … not", so it takes a positive verb: unless you have.

exercises.context: When will we get our grades?
exercises.full_response: They will be posted online by Monday.
exercises.explanation: The grades receive the action, so the passive (will be posted) is required.

exercises.context: Why is the east entrance closed?
exercises.full_response: The stairs are being repaired this week.
exercises.explanation: Present continuous passive: are + being + past participle.

exercises.context: How was the second exam?
exercises.full_response: It was much harder than the first one.
exercises.explanation: Intensify a comparative with "much"; never combine "more" with an -er form.

exercises.context: Should I read all the optional articles?
frame: , the better you'll understand the lectures.
exercises.full_response: The more of them you read, the better you'll understand the lectures.
exercises.explanation: Correlative comparative: "The more … , the better …" with statement order in each half.

exercises.context: Did you enjoy the field trip?
exercises.full_response: I did, even though the weather was terrible.
exercises.explanation: "Even though" introduces a full clause (subject + verb); "in spite of" would need a noun phrase.
